overview.text: Solon was an Athenian lawgiver traditionally associated with reforms around the early sixth century BCE. Athens faced disputes over debt, land, and political privilege. Solon barred the use of people as security for loans and freed Athenians held in debt bondage. He reorganized citizens into property classes that shaped access to public office, while lower-ranked citizens could participate in the assembly. He also revised much of Draco’s earlier, severe law code, retaining its homicide provisions. These changes reduced aristocratic control but did not create full democracy at once. Later Athenians remembered Solon as a foundational reformer, and later reformers built on the political openings he made.

key_facts.text: Solon’s reforms are traditionally placed around 594 BCE, though the precise chronology is debated.
His measures prohibited using a person as security for a loan.
He divided Athenian citizens into four property classes.
Lower-ranked thetes could participate in the assembly but not hold high office.
He retained Draco’s homicide laws while changing much of the rest of that code.

overview.text: Bayezid I, an Ottoman ruler nicknamed “the Thunderbolt,” became sultan after his father Murad I died following the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. He expanded Ottoman power in southeastern Europe and besieged Constantinople, although the city did not fall to him. His forces defeated a crusading army at Nicopolis in 1396, and Bulgaria came under Ottoman control during his reign. His rapid expansion met a major reversal in 1402, when Timur defeated and captured him at the Battle of Ankara. Bayezid died in 1403. His career connects the Ottoman advance in the Balkans with the disruption caused by Timur’s invasion.

key_facts.text: Bayezid I succeeded Murad I in 1389.
His nickname Yıldırım means “the Thunderbolt.”
He besieged Constantinople without capturing it.
Ottoman forces defeated crusaders at Nicopolis in 1396.
Timur captured Bayezid at Ankara in 1402; Bayezid died in 1403.

overview.text: Brexit was the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the European Union. In a June 2016 referendum, a majority of UK voters chose to leave. The government then invoked Article 50 of the EU treaty, beginning a formal withdrawal process. A negotiated withdrawal agreement addressed issues including citizens’ rights and arrangements concerning Ireland and Northern Ireland. The UK ceased to be an EU member on January 31, 2020, but a transition period kept many EU rules applying through December 31 of that year. That distinction matters: membership ended in January, while the single-market and customs-union transition ended in December. The two sides then had to define their future relationship.

key_facts.text: The referendum took place on June 23, 2016.
The UK notified the EU of its intention to leave under Article 50 in March 2017.
The UK stopped being an EU member on January 31, 2020.
EU law continued to apply during the 2020 transition period.
The withdrawal agreement covered citizens’ rights and Ireland/Northern Ireland arrangements.

overview.text: Bastille Day is the common English name for France’s national holiday on July 14. It recalls the storming of the Bastille fortress in Paris in 1789, an event that became a powerful symbol of the French Revolution. The date also evokes the Fête de la Fédération, a gathering held on the storming’s first anniversary in 1790 to celebrate national unity. The modern national holiday was established in 1880, nearly a century after those events. On July 14, 1789, crowds sought gunpowder at the Bastille, which then held only a few prisoners. Its significance lay less in freeing prisoners than in its challenge to royal authority.

key_facts.text: The storming of the Bastille occurred on July 14, 1789.
Parisians sought powder and ammunition at the fortress.
The Bastille held seven prisoners when it fell.
The Fête de la Fédération was held on July 14, 1790.
July 14 became France’s national holiday in 1880.

overview.text: Jawaharlal Nehru was a central leader of India’s struggle for independence and its first prime minister after British rule ended in 1947. As a member and later president of the Indian National Congress, he advocated complete independence and worked alongside Mahatma Gandhi. British authorities jailed him repeatedly for participation in nationalist campaigns, including the Quit India movement during World War II. He served as prime minister from August 15, 1947, until his death in 1964. In office, he promoted a secular democratic state, industrial development, and an international policy that sought room for independent judgment amid Cold War rivalries. His long premiership shaped the institutions of independent India.

key_facts.text: Nehru served as prime minister from August 15, 1947, to May 27, 1964.
He met Gandhi in 1916 and was influenced by him.
At the 1929 Lahore Congress session he presided when complete independence became a goal.
He was imprisoned after the Quit India resolution in 1942.
Nehru promoted industrial development while India sought an independent position in world affairs.

overview.text: The Canadian Conscription Crisis of 1917 was a bitter dispute over drafting men for overseas service in the First World War. Voluntary enlistment no longer supplied enough replacements, so Prime Minister Robert Borden’s government passed the Military Service Act. Support and opposition crossed many communities, but the split was especially sharp between many English-speaking supporters and many French-speaking opponents in Quebec. Conscription became the chief issue in the December 1917 federal election, which Borden’s Unionist government won. Resistance continued into 1918, including deadly rioting in Quebec City. The crisis left lasting political divisions while drafted soldiers eventually strengthened Canadian forces near the war’s end.

key_facts.text: The Military Service Act passed in late August 1917.
The law made men aged 20 to 45 subject to service if called.
Borden’s Unionists won the December 1917 election.
The Unionists lost heavily in Francophone parts of Quebec.
Quebec City experienced deadly anti-conscription rioting at Easter 1918.

overview.text: The Reichstag fire burned Germany’s parliamentary building in Berlin on February 27, 1933, soon after Adolf Hitler became chancellor. Nazi leaders blamed Communists and treated the fire as evidence of a supposed uprising, although the fire’s origins remain disputed. The next day, President Paul von Hindenburg approved an emergency decree that suspended freedoms of speech, press, and assembly and enabled arrests of political opponents. In March, under intimidation and with Communist deputies absent, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, allowing Hitler’s government to make laws without parliament’s consent. The fire itself did not pass that law; its exploitation helped create the conditions for dictatorship.

key_facts.text: The Reichstag building burned on February 27, 1933.
The origins of the fire remain disputed.
The Reichstag Fire Decree was issued on February 28, 1933.
The decree suspended speech, press, and assembly protections.
The March Enabling Act let Hitler’s government legislate without Reichstag consent.

overview.text: Kyiv is Ukraine’s capital and was a political and religious center of medieval Kyivan Rus’. Its surviving monuments show cultural interaction between Kyivan Rus’, the Byzantine Empire, and western Europe. The adoption of Christianity under Prince Volodymyr in 988 shaped its churches and culture. In the early eleventh century, builders constructed Saint Sophia Cathedral under Yaroslav the Wise; its mosaics and frescoes survive as evidence of Kyivan Rus’ art. Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra later became another major religious center. Its medieval religious art influenced buildings beyond Kyiv, while the city remains an important center of Ukrainian history today.

key_facts.text: Kyiv is the capital of modern Ukraine.
Kyiv served as the capital of Kyivan Rus’.
Saint Sophia Cathedral was built under Yaroslav the Wise in the early eleventh century.
The cathedral preserves eleventh-century mosaics and frescoes.
Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra overlooks the Dnipro River.

overview.text: Bartolomeu Dias was a Portuguese navigator whose 1488 voyage rounded the southern end of Africa. He sailed from Lisbon in 1487 with three vessels, seeking a sea passage toward the Indian Ocean and Asia. Storms pushed the fleet away from the coast; when it turned north, it reached the coast east of the cape, showing that ships could pass around Africa. Dias did not sail to India, but his journey made a sea route from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean possible for later Portuguese expeditions. He called the landmark the Cape of Storms; King João II later renamed it the Cape of Good Hope.

key_facts.text: Dias sailed from Lisbon in 1487 with three ships.
He passed Africa’s southern tip in 1488.
His fleet reached Mossel Bay after rounding the cape.
He did not reach India on this voyage.
The Cape of Storms was later called the Cape of Good Hope.

overview.text: The Maginot Line was a French network of forts and defenses built mainly along the eastern frontier between the world wars. Named for War Minister André Maginot, it reflected a strategy of holding a prepared border against attack. Concrete works, gun positions, and underground facilities gave defenders strong local protection, but the system did not form an unbroken shield around France. In May 1940, German forces made their main breakthrough farther north, through the Ardennes and toward Sedan, outflanking the strongest fortifications. The campaign shows that fixed defenses can resist attack where they stand yet fail to prevent an enemy from using a different route.

key_facts.text: The line was a French system of fortified defenses along the Franco-German border.
France built the line chiefly in the interwar period.
The German breakthrough in May 1940 came through the Ardennes.
A May 14, 1940, U.S. diplomatic telegram reported fighting beyond the line’s end near Montmédy.
The line’s presence did not stop Germany’s 1940 invasion of France.
